_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for North Korea (DPRK) covering ancient Gojoseon, Three Kingdoms (Goguryeo), Unified Silla, Goryeo, Joseon Dynasty, Japanese colonization 1910-1945, post-WWII Soviet occupation zone, Kim Il Sung's Korean War (1950-53, ceasefire only), Juche ideology, totalitarian state, famine 1990s, nuclear weapons program (2006+ tests), hereditary dictatorship (Kim dynasty), cult of personality, and extreme isolation.

country_profile.government_type: Unitary one-party totalitarian Juche socialist republic

population.source: UN estimate (DPRK does not release reliable data)

gdp.source: CIA World Factbook (last estimate, highly uncertain)

religion.note: Officially atheist state; religion brutally suppressed; Juche ideology (Kim Il Sung's self-reliance philosophy) is quasi-religious state cult; Kim family worshipped; Songbun (songbun) caste system based on family background; underground Christianity persecuted

ethnic_groups.name: Korean
ethnic_groups.notes: Ethnically homogeneous; totalitarian state enforces extreme nationalism; 'pure blood' ideology; Han Chinese small minority (mostly traders at border); hermit kingdom

independence.from: Declared independence from Soviet/US occupation zones after WWII Japanese colonial rule ended; separate from South Korea

country_profile.notes_unique: Most isolated/totalitarian state globally; nuclear weapons state (6 tests 2006-2017); ICBMs; Juche ideology; hereditary dictatorship (Kim dynasty, 3 generations); Korean War (1950-53, ~3M dead, technically still at war - armistice only); 1990s famine ('Arduous March', ~1M dead); gulags (kwanliso camps, ~120,000 prisoners); no internet (Kwangmyong intranet only); propaganda/personality cult; Ryugyong Hotel (tallest unoccupied building globally, 1987-incomplete)

current_leader.name: Kim Jong Un
current_leader.title: Supreme Leader (General Secretary of WPK, President of State Affairs Commission, Supreme Commander of Armed Forces)
current_leader.notes: Third-generation hereditary dictator; grandson of Kim Il Sung; purged uncle Jang Song-thaek (2013); possibly killed half-brother Kim Jong-nam (2017 assassination Malaysia); nuclear/ICBM tests; summits with Trump (2018-19); COVID-19 hermit seal; sister Kim Yo-jong key aide

former_leaders.name: Kim Jong Il
former_leaders.notes: 'Dear Leader'; son of Kim Il Sung; cult of personality; Songun (military-first) policy; 1990s famine; collapsed economy; nuclear program; second-generation dictator; died of heart attack on train

former_leaders.name: Kim Il Sung
former_leaders.notes: 'Eternal President'; founded DPRK; Korean War (invaded South 1950); totalitarian state builder; Juche ideology; extreme personality cult ('Sun of the Nation'); massive statues/portraits mandatory; continues to be 'president' posthumously

910.name: Gojoseon and Early Korean Kingdoms
910.description: The legendary founding of Gojoseon by Dangun, the first Korean state, the Chinese Han Commanderies, and the emergence of the Proto-Three Kingdoms period.

sub_clusters.name: Gojoseon Kingdom
sub_clusters.description: The semi-legendary kingdom of Gojoseon centered in Manchuria and northern Korea, the Dangun founding myth, Wiman Joseon, and the Han dynasty's conquest establishing four commanderies.
key_events: Legendary founding of Gojoseon by Dangun Wanggeom (traditional date 2333 BC)
Han Emperor Wu conquers Wiman Joseon and establishes the Four Commanderies (108 BC)

sub_clusters.name: Han Commanderies and Buyeo
sub_clusters.description: The Chinese Lelang Commandery as a center of Chinese culture in northern Korea, the Buyeo kingdom in Manchuria, and the emergence of native Korean polities resisting Chinese control.

910.name: Goguryeo Kingdom
910.description: The powerful northern Korean kingdom of Goguryeo, renowned for its warrior culture, magnificent tomb murals, resistance to Chinese invasion, and its pivotal role in the Three Kingdoms of Korea.

sub_clusters.name: Goguryeo Rise and Expansion
sub_clusters.description: The founding by Jumong, the conquest of the Lelang Commandery, King Gwanggaeto the Great's vast territorial expansion, and Goguryeo's emergence as the dominant power in northeast Asia.
key_events: King Gwanggaeto the Great expands Goguryeo to its maximum extent across Manchuria and Korea (391–413 AD)

sub_clusters.name: Goguryeo-Sui/Tang Wars and Fall
sub_clusters.description: Goguryeo's heroic resistance against massive Sui and Tang invasions, General Eulji Mundeok's annihilation of a Sui army, Yang Manchun's defense of Ansi Fortress, and the final Tang-Silla conquest.
key_events: General Eulji Mundeok destroys Sui Emperor Yang's 300,000-strong army at the Salsu River (612)
Tang-Silla alliance conquers Goguryeo after prolonged resistance (668)

910.name: Balhae Kingdom
910.description: The successor kingdom to Goguryeo in Manchuria and northern Korea, known as the 'Flourishing Land of the East,' which maintained Goguryeo's cultural traditions until its conquest by the Khitan.

sub_clusters.name: Balhae Foundation and Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: Dae Joyeong's founding of Balhae from Goguryeo refugees, the expansion of territory, sophisticated diplomatic relations with Tang China and Japan, and the height of cultural achievement.
key_events: Dae Joyeong founds Balhae, claiming succession from Goguryeo (698)

sub_clusters.name: Balhae Decline and Khitan Conquest
sub_clusters.description: The weakening of Balhae through internal strife, the devastating Khitan invasion and conquest, and the mass migration of Balhae refugees to Goryeo Korea.

920.name: Goryeo Dynasty — Northern Territories
920.description: The Goryeo dynasty's claim to the Goguryeo heritage, the defense of the northern frontier against Khitan and Jurchen invasions, the Mongol subjugation, and the legacy in the modern North Korean region.

sub_clusters.name: Goryeo-Khitan Wars
sub_clusters.description: Three major Khitan Liao invasions of Goryeo and the heroic Korean resistance, culminating in General Gang Gam-chan's decisive victory at the Battle of Gwiju.
key_events: General Gang Gam-chan annihilates the Khitan army at the Battle of Gwiju (1019)

sub_clusters.name: Mongol Invasions of Goryeo
sub_clusters.description: Six devastating Mongol invasions of Korea, the court's retreat to Ganghwa Island, the carving of the Tripitaka Koreana, and Goryeo's eventual submission as a Mongol vassal state.
key_events: Tripitaka Koreana — over 80,000 woodblocks carved as a prayer for divine aid against the Mongols (1236–1251)

920.name: Joseon Dynasty — Northern Regions
920.description: The Joseon dynasty's administration of the northern provinces, frontier defense, the Jurchen/Manchu relations, and the distinctive culture of the Hamgyeong and Pyeongan provinces.

sub_clusters.name: Six Garrisons and Northern Frontier
sub_clusters.description: King Sejong's establishment of the Six Garrisons along the Tumen River, the expansion of the northern border, the Jurchen campaigns, and the Manchu invasions of Korea.
key_events: King Sejong establishes the Six Garrisons, fixing Korea's northern border at the Yalu and Tumen Rivers (1434–1443)

sub_clusters.name: Late Joseon Northern Provinces
sub_clusters.description: Regional discrimination against the northwest, the Hong Gyeongnae Rebellion, Russian encroachment on the Tumen frontier, and the northern provinces' reputation as a stronghold of resistance.

930.name: Japanese Colonial Rule in the North
930.description: The Japanese colonial period in northern Korea, with its focus on heavy industrialization, resource extraction, the anti-Japanese partisan movement, and the emergence of Kim Il-sung.

sub_clusters.name: Colonial Industrialization
sub_clusters.description: Japan's transformation of northern Korea into an industrial base with hydroelectric dams, chemical plants, and steel mills, creating the most industrialized region on the Korean Peninsula.
key_events: Supung Dam on the Yalu River — one of the largest hydroelectric dams in Asia at the time (1937–1941)

sub_clusters.name: Anti-Japanese Resistance and Kim Il-sung
sub_clusters.description: The Manchurian partisan guerrilla movement, Kim Il-sung's emergence as a resistance leader, the Battle of Pochonbo, and the Soviet training of Korean communists.
key_events: Kim Il-sung leads the raid on Pochonbo — a key event in DPRK founding mythology (1937)

940.name: Division of Korea and the Korean War
940.description: The Soviet occupation of northern Korea, the establishment of the DPRK under Kim Il-sung, the invasion of the South, the devastating Korean War, and the armistice dividing the peninsula.

sub_clusters.name: Soviet Occupation and DPRK Founding
sub_clusters.description: The Soviet occupation north of the 38th parallel, Kim Il-sung's installation as leader, the establishment of the Korean Workers' Party, and the proclamation of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
key_events: Korea divided at the 38th parallel between Soviet and American occupation zones (1945)
Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) proclaimed with Kim Il-sung as Premier (September 9, 1948)

sub_clusters.name: Korean War
sub_clusters.description: Kim Il-sung's invasion of the South, the near-total UN/US counteroffensive, Chinese intervention, three years of devastating warfare, and the armistice at Panmunjom.
key_events: North Korea invades the South — Korean War begins (June 25, 1950)
Chinese People's Volunteer Army enters the war, pushing UN forces south (October 1950)
Armistice signed at Panmunjom — the war ends in stalemate (July 27, 1953)

950.name: Kim Il-sung Era
950.description: Kim Il-sung's construction of the Juche state, the cult of personality, initial postwar economic success, the Sino-Soviet split balancing act, and the transformation into the world's most isolated state.

sub_clusters.name: Postwar Reconstruction and Juche
sub_clusters.description: The Chollima Movement for rapid reconstruction, the promulgation of Juche (self-reliance) ideology, the purge of all rival factions, and North Korea's initial economic outperformance of the South.
key_events: Kim Il-sung promulgates Juche as the DPRK's guiding ideology (1955–1972)

sub_clusters.name: Kim Il-sung Personality Cult and Stagnation
sub_clusters.description: The 1972 constitution making Kim president for life, the USS Pueblo incident, the Rangoon bombing, the preparation of Kim Jong-il as successor, economic decline, and Kim Il-sung's death.
key_events: USS Pueblo seized by North Korea (1968)
Kim Il-sung dies — Kim Jong-il inherits power in the first communist dynastic succession (July 8, 1994)

960.name: Kim Jong-il and Kim Jong-un Eras
960.description: The famine of the 1990s, nuclear weapons development, the Songun military-first policy, Kim Jong-un's succession, nuclear and missile tests, and brief diplomatic openings.

sub_clusters.name: Arduous March Famine
sub_clusters.description: The catastrophic North Korean famine following the collapse of Soviet aid and floods, with an estimated 600,000 to 2.5 million deaths, the Agreed Framework nuclear deal, and the Songun policy.
key_events: North Korean famine ('Arduous March') kills hundreds of thousands (1994–1998)
Agreed Framework — North Korea freezes nuclear program in exchange for aid (1994)

sub_clusters.name: Nuclear Weapons and Kim Jong-un
sub_clusters.description: North Korea's nuclear tests, Kim Jong-un's succession and purges including the execution of Jang Song-thaek, ICBM development, the 2018 Singapore summit with Trump, and continued isolation.
key_events: North Korea conducts its first nuclear test (October 2006)
Kim Jong-un meets President Trump in Singapore — first US-DPRK summit (June 2018)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
